say: You give it a test statistic, $z$. It tells you how likely a result **this far out** is if the claim were true.
The key idea: look up the tail area in the tables and, for a two-tailed test, **double** it. If the $p$-value is under $0.05$, reject the claim.

how.higher: It is the last part of a hypothesis test on Paper 2, worth 5 to 10 marks. You are asked for the p-value and then for a conclusion in words, and sometimes the question runs backwards from a given p-value to a sample mean.

example.question: A machine is set to fill bags with a mean mass of $500$ g and a standard deviation of $12$ g. A sample of $36$ bags has a mean mass of $504.6$ g. Test, at the $5\%$ level, whether the mean mass has changed. Use a $p$-value.

steps.title: Find the test statistic
steps.say: Standardise the sample mean to find $\hl{1}{z}$. The spread of a sample mean is $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$, not $\sigma$.

steps.title: Read the tables
steps.say: Look up $P(z < 2.3)$ in the normal tables.

steps.title: Double the tail
steps.say: The test is two-tailed, so $\hl{2}{p}$ counts both tails. Take the tail above $2.3$ and double it.

steps.title: Compare and conclude
steps.say: Compare $\hl{2}{p}$ with $0.05$. Then say what it means for the claim, in the words of the question.

lines.text: $p$ is less than $0.05$, so reject the claim. There is evidence that the mean mass of the bags has changed.

workedSolution.finalAnswer: p = 0.0214 < 0.05 \text{, so the mean mass has changed}

higher.tip: Finish with a conclusion in words that refers back to the question. A $p$-value with no conclusion, or one that ignores the context, loses marks.

higher.tip: For a two-tailed test, double the tail. Write the doubling as its own line: $2[1 - P(z < \dots)]$ earns marks of its own.
If your working compares $z$ with $\pm 1.96$ instead of using a $p$-value, the conclusion is still accepted. Use whichever the question asks for.
When the question gives you the $p$-value and asks for the sample mean, use the direction of the change to pick the sign of $z$.

say: You give it what you want from a confidence interval: a confidence level, or a target margin of error. It tells you whether the interval gets **wider** or narrower, or how big the sample must be.
The key idea: the margin is $z\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}$, so it grows with the confidence level and shrinks with $\sqrt{n}$. Halving the margin needs **four times** the sample.

how.higher: It appears on Paper 2 inside the confidence-interval question: once as a 10-mark part that sets the margin of error and asks for the sample size, and once as a table of always, sometimes or never true statements about the width.

example.question: In a poll, $40\%$ of the people sampled support a proposal. A $95\%$ confidence interval for the proportion who support it must have a margin of error of at most $0.03$. Find the smallest sample size, $n$, that does this.

steps.title: Set up the margin of error
steps.say: The margin of error is the part added to and taken from $\hat p$: $1.96\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}$. Put in $\hat p = 0.4$ and set the margin equal to $0.03$ to find the borderline $\hl{1}{n}$.

steps.title: Square both sides
steps.say: Square to remove the root, then $n$ can be brought up from the bottom.

steps.title: Solve for n
steps.say: Swap $n$ and the square, then work it out.

lines.text: A bigger $n$ gives a smaller margin, and $n$ must be a whole number. Round **up**.

higher.tip: Subtract to find the margin first. Finding $0.085$ (the difference between the end of the interval and $\hat p$) is a step the marks are tied to.
Use the full margin $1.96\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}$ when you know $\hat p$. The shortcut $1/\sqrt{n}$ caps your marks at mid partial credit.

higher.tip: Round the sample size correctly. Rounding in the wrong direction costs a mark.
For the widest possible margin, find the $\hat p$ that makes $\hat p(1-\hat p)$ biggest. Calculus or completing the square both earn marks.

say: You give it a value $x$ from a normal distribution with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$. It gives back $z$, the number of standard deviations $x$ sits **above or below** the mean.
The key idea: $z$ puts any normal distribution on one common scale, so you can read the tables, or compare two values from different distributions.

how.higher: It is the first step of nearly every normal-distribution part on Paper 2, from 2016 to 2025. Standardise first, then use the tables to find a probability, a percentage, or a missing value. It is also tested alone when two scores must be compared.

example.question: The marks in an exam are normally distributed with mean $58$ and standard deviation $12$. Find the percentage of students who scored more than $73$.

steps.title: Find the z-score
steps.say: Standardise: take away the mean, then divide by the standard deviation. This gives $\hl{1}{z}$.

steps.title: Read the tables
steps.say: The tables give the area to the **left** of $z$. Look up $P(z < 1.25)$.

steps.title: Take the area on the right
steps.say: We want the students above $73$, so take the left area from $1$.

lines.text: About $10.6\%$ of the students scored more than $73$.

higher.tip: Write $z = \frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$ with the numbers put in. Even some correct substitution earns partial credit.
Draw the normal curve and mark the mean and the value. A sketch with relevant work on it is credited.

higher.tip: To compare two scores, find the $z$-score of each, then say which is higher in words.

say: You give it a mean, $\mu$, and a standard deviation, $\sigma$. It tells you what share of a normal distribution lies within **1, 2 or 3** standard deviations of the mean: $68\%$, $95\%$ and $99.7\%$.
The key idea: count how many $\sigma$ a value is from $\mu$. The curve is symmetrical, so the leftover share splits equally between the two tails.

how.higher: It is used only now and then on Paper 2, as a quick estimate: the percentage between two values a whole number of standard deviations from the mean, or the values at the steps of a table.
how.ordinary: It is on Paper 2 almost every year, as a 5 to 15 mark part. You fill in a normal curve, find a percentage or a number of people, or work back from a range holding 95% to the mean and standard deviation.

example.question: The lifetime of a battery is normally distributed with mean $60$ hours and standard deviation $5$ hours. Use the empirical rule to find the percentage of batteries that last more than $70$ hours.

steps.title: Count the standard deviations
steps.say: Find how far $70$ is above the mean, then divide by $\sigma$. This is how many $\hl{1}{\sigma}$ away it is.

lines.text: So $70$ is $2$ standard deviations above the mean.

steps.title: Use the rule
steps.say: The empirical rule says $95\%$ of values lie within $2$ standard deviations of the mean. That is between $50$ and $70$ hours.

steps.title: Share out the tails
steps.say: The rest lies outside, in the two tails. We want only the **upper** tail, so split it in half.

higher.tip: Say how many standard deviations each value is from the mean. Showing that link between deviation and mean earns marks.

higher.tip: The rule and the tables give slightly different answers (81.5% and 81.85%). Either method is accepted.

ordinary.tip: Shade the area you want on the curve. It earns marks even if the final answer is wrong.
